selected_mechanism.name: FCC Alaska Plan Expiration and Alaska Connect Fund September 1 Performance Plan Filing Gate

news_trigger.headline: The FCC sends billions to Alaska companies selling slow internet. You pay for it.
news_trigger.verbatim_span: In 2016, the FCC created a program called the Alaska Plan specifically for carriers here, allowing them to negotiate their own performance targets rather than being subject to the same cost models applied elsewhere.

selected_mechanism.one_line_definition: The Alaska Plan — a 10-year, $1.5 billion federal universal service program that let thirteen Alaska mobile and rate-of-return carriers negotiate individualized performance plans instead of national cost models — expires December 31, 2026, and any carrier that does not file an Alaska Connect Fund performance plan with the FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau by September 1, 2026 loses support immediately, with no grace period for the initial cutoff; the WTB Chief then holds binary approval authority over each plan, determining whether the carrier receives support through 2034 or exits the federal subsidy stack entirely.

layers.layer_name: L1 — FCC ETC Designation and Alaska Plan Authorization
layers.what_it_does: Establishes which carriers are eligible telecommunications carriers under the Alaska Plan and grants them access to the high-cost universal service fund; only FCC-designated ETCs may receive support. The Alaska Plan waived national cost-model requirements for the 13 opt-in carriers, creating individualized performance obligation tracks.
layers.controlling_actor: FCC Wireline Competition Bureau (ETC designation authority for non-rural carriers); Alaska Plan established under 47 CFR 54.317

layers.layer_name: L2 — USAC High-Cost Fund Disbursement Administration
layers.what_it_does: Universal Service Administrative Company, as the FCC-designated administrator, calculates and disburses monthly Alaska Plan support payments to each carrier based on their approved performance plan and certification compliance. USAC is the payment chokepoint between FCC policy and carrier cash flow.
layers.controlling_actor: USAC (not-for-profit corporation, FCC-designated under 47 CFR 54.701); High-Cost Program Division

layers.what_it_does: The Alaska Plan's statutory 10-year authorization ends December 31, 2026. All 13 participating carriers face simultaneous support termination unless they separately opt into the Alaska Connect Fund successor program. This is the structural forcing function that creates the binary: file by September 1 or exit.
layers.controlling_actor: 13 Alaska ETCs including GCI Communications (largest disbursement recipient), GCI-affiliated entities, and smaller rate-of-return carriers

layers.layer_name: L4 — Alaska Connect Fund September 1, 2026 Performance Plan Opt-In Filing
layers.what_it_does: Mobile ETCs must submit individualized performance plans to the FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau by September 1, 2026 to be eligible for Alaska Connect Fund support beginning January 1, 2027. Under 47 CFR 54.318, carriers that miss this deadline have support end December 31, 2026 with a 24-month phase-down; carriers without approved plans by December 31, 2026 face support delay. The plan must specify 5G-NR deployment obligations, coverage hexagons, and technology standards.
layers.controlling_actor: Carrier regulatory teams (GCI Communications regulatory affairs; individual rate-of-return carrier executives) — the filing obligation is on each carrier; no federal agent files on their behalf

layers.layer_name: L5 — FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau Review and Binary Approval
layers.what_it_does: The WTB Chief reviews each filed performance plan and issues a binary approval or rejection. An approved plan locks in the carrier's support level, coverage commitments, and technology obligations through 2034 (single-support areas) or 2029 (duplicate-support areas). A rejection or non-filing means support termination — the WTB has no obligation to negotiate or extend. The WTB also adjudicates carrier requests to modify performance obligations on technical/financial feasibility grounds.
layers.controlling_actor: FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau Chief (institutional role; current incumbent under Chair Brendan Carr's FCC)

chokepoint.layer_name: L5 — FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau Review and Binary Approval
chokepoint.controlling_actor: FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau Chief (institutional role under the Commission)
chokepoint.binary_decision: Approve or reject each Alaska Connect Fund performance plan. Approval = carrier receives federal support through 2034 at the committed level. Rejection or non-approval by December 31, 2026 = support delayed or terminated. No other federal or state actor can override this determination within the WTB's delegated authority.
chokepoint.why_asymmetric: The WTB Chief acts under delegated Commission authority and issues final bureau-level decisions on performance plan approvals without requiring a full FCC vote. This is a single institutional officer — not a five-member Commission vote, not a committee — holding binary authority over each carrier's multi-year federal subsidy stream. The September 1 filing deadline is fixed in 47 CFR 54.318 with no regulatory grace mechanism; missed filing flows directly to the WTB's approval calendar, making the bureau's review window (September 1 to December 31, 2026) the only remaining gate before support terminates.

selected_mechanism.structural_read: The Alaska Plan was designed as a 10-year workaround that let Alaska carriers escape the national cost-model discipline applied everywhere else in the country, in exchange for individualized performance commitments the FCC could not practically enforce. The ADN/ProPublica investigation documents what that produced: $4.6 billion disbursed, Alaska still near the bottom for fixed broadband, and at least one carrier receiving $10,000/year per subscriber while providing functionally no service. The Alaska Connect Fund transition does not fix the structural problem — it extends it to 2034 with 5G-NR obligations — but the September 1, 2026 filing gate is the first moment in a decade where the FCC WTB can actually condition continued subsidy on a specific forward commitment. Carriers that file get locked into hexagon-level coverage obligations they cannot renegotiate easily. Carriers that do not file lose hundreds of millions in annualized support. Either outcome reshapes the rural Alaska broadband landscape in ways that determine where AI-adjacent infrastructure (edge compute, connected fisheries monitoring, remote sensing relays) can realistically deploy in the 2027-2030 timeframe.
selected_mechanism.forward_implication: Any operator, enterprise, or state agency planning rural Alaska AI or broadband-dependent infrastructure in communities served by Alaska Plan ETCs should obtain written confirmation from each carrier of its September 1 filing status before committing capital to site selection or service-level agreements — a carrier that misses the deadline and exits the subsidy stack may immediately reprice or discontinue service in marginal-cost rural markets, stranding collocated infrastructure investment.
selected_mechanism.ak_consequence: GCI Communications (largest Alaska ETC by disbursement share, 207,000 wireless lines, ~$935M annual revenue) must file an approved Alaska Connect Fund performance plan with the FCC WTB by September 1, 2026 or face federal support termination December 31, 2026 — a loss that would directly pressure the carrier's rural Alaska 5G deployment commitments and its ability to provide the wireless backhaul on which Aleutian, Western, and Interior community broadband access depends through at least 2034.
